rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Māʾidah is a Madinan sūrah, and some of its verses were among the last revelations received by the Prophet Muhammad.
rows.anchor: A Madinan sūrah, al-Māʾidah contains verses that are considered to be among the last that the Prophet Muhammad received

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All verses of al-Māʾidah were revealed after the conquest of Makkah in 8/630.
rows.anchor: all of its verses were revealed after the conquest of Makkah in 8/630 (Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Māʾidah is described as one of the last complete sūrahs revealed to the Prophet, alongside al-Fatḥ.
rows.anchor: The sūrah itself is one of the last

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr’s cited view places al-Naṣr among the candidates for the last complete sūrah revealed.
rows.anchor: believed to have been the last (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 5:3 is one of several verses variously reported as the last the Prophet received before his death; others include 2:281, 4:176, 9:128–29, and 110:1–3.
rows.anchor: variously reported to be the last that the Prophet received

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 5:3 and other verses in the sūrah were reportedly revealed during the Prophet’s Farewell Pilgrimage sermon in 10/632.
rows.anchor: This verse and several others in the sūrah were reportedly revealed in the course of the Prophet’s parting sermon during the Farewell Pilgrimage in 10/632 (Q, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports say the Prophet received the sūrah while riding a camel, whose inability to bear the descent’s weight required him to dismount.
rows.anchor: while he was riding on a camel. The camel could not bear the weight of its descent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is named for the miraculous food-laden table God sends to Jesus and his apostles at their request in 5:112–115.
rows.anchor: sūrah takes its name from the miraculous table spread with food (al-māʾidah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening verses prescribe pilgrimage, lawful foods, intermarriage, and ritual purity.
rows.anchor: pilgrimage, lawful foods, intermarriage, and ritual purity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These opening rulings are interspersed with reminders of God’s blessings on the Muslim community and the need to fulfill the covenant with Him.
rows.anchor: interspersed with reminders of God’s blessings upon the Muslim community and of the necessity of fulfilling the covenant with Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening lines have a triumphant, hopeful tone and, through their emphasis on blessings and covenant, recall Moses’ final sermon in Deuteronomy.
rows.anchor: tone of these opening lines is religiously triumphant and hopeful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening’s repeated emphasis on blessings and covenant is compared with Moses’ final sermon as recounted in Deuteronomy.
rows.anchor: bears some comparison with Moses’ final sermon as recounted in the Biblical book of Deuteronomy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One major concern of the sūrah is to establish definitive ritual and legal rulings, owing to its late revelation.
rows.anchor: ritual and legal rulings considered to be definitive by virtue of the late revelation of the sūrah

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī’s cited view is that no ruling in al-Māʾidah was ever abrogated.
rows.anchor: Some assert that no ruling in this sūrah was ever abrogated (Q)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr’s cited view is that parts of 5:2 and 5:106 were abrogated.
rows.anchor: some claim that parts of v. 2 and v. 106 have been abrogated (IK).

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reportedly said that because al-Māʾidah was revealed late, its permissions should be treated as licit and its prohibitions as forbidden.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is reported to have said, “O people! Sūrat al-Māʾidah

rows.speaker: ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: A similar statement about al-Māʾidah’s permissions and prohibitions is attributed to the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah.
rows.anchor: a similar statement is attributed to the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah (IK, Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its rulings include pilgrimage prescriptions in 5:1–2 and 5:95–97.
rows.anchor: Its rulings include prescriptions concerning the pilgrimage or ḥajj

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its rulings include dietary law in 5:3–5 and 5:87–88.
rows.anchor: dietary law (vv. 3–5, 87–88)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its rulings address wine and gambling in 5:90–91.
rows.anchor: wine and gambling (vv.90–91)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its rulings include provisions for making bequests in 5:106–108.
rows.anchor: making bequests (vv. 106–8)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah sets legal punishments for those who wage war against God and His Messenger and seek to spread corruption on earth.
rows.anchor: establishes the legal punishments (ḥudūd; sing. ḥadd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These punishments are understood to concern exceedingly violent crimes against the community, including armed robbery and aggression.
rows.anchor: understood to pertain to exceedingly violent crimes against the community, including armed robbery and aggression (vv. 33–34)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah also establishes legal punishments for theft.
rows.anchor: as well as theft (vv. 38–39)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to prayer appears only at 5:58, which mentions it without using the technical term adhān.
rows.anchor: mentioned exclusively in v. 58, although it does not refer to it by its technical term, adhān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah’s second and larger concern is to establish relations between the Muslim community and the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: The second and larger issue with which the sūrah is concerned is the definitive establishment of relations between the Muslim community and the People of the Book.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jews and Christians are criticized for breaking or forgetting their covenants with God.
rows.anchor: They are accused of breaking or forgetting their covenants with God (vv. 12–14)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Christians are chastised for exaggerated claims of divinity for Jesus and his mother.
rows.anchor: Christians are chastised for exaggerated claims of divinity for Jesus and his mother (vv.17–18, 116)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah recounts the Israelites’ refusal to obey Moses’ command to fight.
rows.anchor: the Israelites’ refusal to obey Moses’ command to fight is recounted (vv. 20–26)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 5:5 permits Muslims to eat the People of the Book’s food and marry their women, allowing substantial social relations.
rows.anchor: in v. 5, Muslims are allowed to eat their food and to marry women from among them, thereby allowing for substantial social relations between Muslims and the People of the Book.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 5:51–57 set political boundaries by warning Muslims against taking Jews and Christians as protectors to the exclusion of their own religious community.
rows.anchor: in vv. 51–57, political boundaries are established between these communities, as Muslims are warned not to take Jews and Christians as protectors to the exclusion of members of the Muslim religious community

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic Law allows treaties of alliance between Muslim states and Christian or Jewish political entities.
rows.anchor: Islamic Law does allow treaties of alliance between the Muslim state, or states, and Christian or Jewish political entities).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 5:41–47 concern the Prophet’s and, by extension, the Islamic state’s authority to judge legal disputes among the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: Vv. 41–47 concern the ability of the Prophet, and by extension the authority of the Islamic state, to render judgment in legal disputes among the People of the Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jewish and Christian communities each have their own law and way.
rows.anchor: they also establish that these two communities have their own “law and way” (v. 48)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The People of the Book should judge themselves according to their own scriptures.
rows.anchor: they should judge themselves according to their own scriptures (vv. 43–47)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 5:82–85 offer a positive portrait of Christian devotion.
rows.anchor: Vv. 82–85 present a beautiful portrait of Christian devotion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The end recounts Jesus’ extraordinary miracles, including the unique descent of the table spread from Heaven, and warns about Christians who disbelieved afterward.
rows.anchor: Heaven—but concludes with a warning about those Christians

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah closes with a statement of God’s complete sovereignty and power over all things.
rows.anchor: The sūrah ends with a final statement of God’s complete Sovereignty and Power over all things.
